blocks.text: Aldehydes are prepared by the oxidation of primary alcohols with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or acidified KMnO₄.

In the example of the preparation of ethanol, the acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ is added drop wise to the warm ethanol. The aldehyde produced is distilled off as soon as it is formed. This prevents the further oxidation of ethanal to ethanoic acids. The temperature is kept above the boiling point of acetaldehyde but below to that of ethanol, since ethanol has higher boiling point than that of acetaldehyde. Pure ethanal is obtained by redistillation. Ketones are also prepared by the same procedure from secondary alcohols but since ketones are not converted into carboxylic acids under these conditions, therefore ketone is not distilled off immediately.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The example is the preparation of ethanal (the aldehyde) from ethanol; ethanol is the starting alcohol, not the product.

blocks.alt: Apparatus: a round flask of H2SO4(aq) in a water or oil bath at a temperature higher than the b.p. of the aldehyde, heated from below. A tilted dropping funnel in a side neck adds K2Cr2O7(aq) and alcohol slowly. A thermometer in the top neck has its bulb at the side arm. A sloping condenser (water in at the lower end, water out at the upper end) leads to a test tube of aldehyde distillate.
blocks.caption: Figure 23.1: Apparatus for distilling off the ethanal as it is formed by the oxidation of ethanol (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 23.1).

blocks.text: Methanol, HCHO, is a gas at room temperature. It is often encountered as a 40 % aqueous solution called 'formalin', which has a fishy, unpleasant smell and is used for preserving biological specimens. Other short-chain aldehydes and ketones are liquids.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: HCHO is methanal (formaldehyde), not methanol (CH₃OH). Formalin has a sharp, pungent smell, not a fishy one.
